title: Fret Board
primary_metric: total shop time, in minutes, to calculate, mark, and cut all 22 frets (shared cutting/installing/dressing time plus each method's own per-fret calculation time)

options.A: Mark every fret using the Precision Method — the exact twelfth-root-of-two ratio, calculated to four decimal places at each fret
options.B: Mark every fret using the Rule of Eighteen — the traditional whole-number-divisor shortcut

sources.claim: Exact formula for fret distance from the nut under equal temperament, and the numeric value of the twelfth root of two
sources.value: distance(n) = L x [1 - (1/2)^(n/12)]; twelfth root of two ~= 1.0594630943593
sources.title: Calculating Fret Positions
sources.note: Standard equal-temperament fret formula, algebraically equivalent to the iterative StewMac form. No publication date on the source page; graded HIGH because the figure is a fixed mathematical definition, not a claim that could go stale.

sources.claim: The modern, more precise fret-spacing divisor (17.817154) some shops use instead of the traditional 18
sources.title: Fret Scale Rule Instructions
sources.note: Used only as contextual background in Appendix C (explaining that the shop's own 'rule of 18' shortcut is a rounding of this more precise constant) -- NOT the divisor used to compute Appendix C's own table, which correctly models the historical whole-number rule of 18 per S3.

sources.claim: The traditional 'rule of 18' historically used an exact whole-number divisor of 18, and produces frets that trend flat of true equal temperament
sources.title: Was the Rule of 18 Good Enough?
sources.note: Confirms the divisor is exactly 18 in the traditional method (not a rounding of 17.817 in the source itself), and that the resulting frets trend flat of true equal temperament -- both facts used in Appendix C/D. The article does not give an exact cents figure at fret 12; that figure is derived (see below), consistent with this source's qualitative finding.

sources.claim: Named standard guitar scale lengths and typical modern-electric fret-count range
sources.value: Fender-style 25.5 in; Gibson-style 24.75 in; PRS-style 25 in; 21-24 frets typical for modern electric guitars
sources.title: Guitar Scale Length Explained
sources.note: Scale length (25.5 in, Fender-style) is used directly as this build's spec. Fret-count range (21-24) is used only as the basis for Modeling Assumption MA2, not as a directly-claimed figure, since the exact count for THIS build is a scenario choice.

sources.claim: A real professional repair-shop job-costing example, showing shops estimate fret work in fractional hours rather than a fixed price; one cited line item is roughly 0.6 hours for the fret-installation portion of a comparable refret job
sources.value: 0.6 hours (fret-installation line item, one example job)
sources.title: Guitar repair money talk: estimate hours, not dollars
sources.note: Used only as directional, order-of-magnitude context for Modeling Assumption MA6's 45-minute shared cutting/installing/dressing baseline -- NOT used as the value itself (this build's job is a fresh-neck fret job, not the repair-refret job in the source's example, and the source's figure covers only the fret-installation step, not slotting/dressing). Graded MEDIUM confidence because it is one real professional's one example line item, not a general trade standard. MA6's value_used (45 minutes) is a reasoned scenario estimate, not this sourced figure restated.

deliverables.text: A fret-position table, Precision Method: distance from the nut for frets 1-12 using the twelfth-root-of-two ratio, to four decimal places.
A fret-position table, Rule of Eighteen: distance from the nut for frets 1-12 using the traditional whole-number-divisor shortcut.
A cents-of-deviation conversion at fret 12, using the D1/D2 length difference and the cents formula in Appendix D.
A GCF string-length-ratio table for frets 1-5, reduced to lowest terms, identifying which frets land on simple whole-number ratios.
A recommendation comparing both methods' 12th-fret deviation against the acceptable intonation tolerance and the re-fret cost.

balance.argument_a: Even though the Precision Method's per-fret arithmetic takes a little longer to work out by hand (evaluating a fractional twelfth-root-of-two exponent on a scientific calculator has more keystrokes and more chance of a keying slip than simple division), that calculation time is a small fraction of the total job once the shared, method-independent time to cut, install, and dress all 22 frets is counted (Appendix F). The Precision Method is also exact by construction at fret 12 -- it lands exactly at half the scale length, matching true equal temperament with zero drift, with zero re-fret risk regardless of what the tolerance line turns out to be.
balance.argument_b: The Rule of Eighteen's simpler iterative arithmetic (repeated division and running subtraction, the same shortcut proportional dividers were built to avoid doing by hand) computes faster per fret, and it is the method generations of working luthiers actually used on instruments that intonated well enough to play professionally. Its total shop time across all 22 frets is measurably lower than the Precision Method's. The tradeoff is a known, named accuracy cost -- about 12.5 cents flat at fret 12, roughly 2.5x the stated MA1 tolerance -- disclosed and quantified in Appendix D, not hidden.
balance.margin_basis: Compare each option's total shop time in minutes (Appendix F): the shared, method-independent baseline time to cut/install/dress all 22 frets (MA6) plus each method's own per-fret calculation time (MA4 for Option A, MA5 for Option B), summed across 22 frets.
balance.margin_note: RETUNED 2026-08-27, case-write-stage remediation, case-owner decision -- see cases/fret-board/QA_REPORT.md's 2026-08-26 case-readiness run and its 'Judgment call for a human' section. That run found this case's ORIGINAL primary metric -- cents of pitch deviation from true equal temperament at fret 12 -- structurally unbalanceable under SPEC §2: Option A (Precision Method) is exact by construction, 0 cents, at EVERY fret, not just fret 12 (verified by hand: at fret 1 the Precision Method's own 4-decimal rounding error is on the order of 0.000004 cents, versus the Rule of Eighteen's ~1.04 cents/fret systematic drift -- an earlier-fret regrade, the QA report's first suggested repair, does not fix the imbalance, since ANY nonzero Option-B cents figure against an exact-zero Option A always computes to a 100% margin under this project's loser/winner formula). Retuning within the accuracy axis was therefore ruled out as dishonest (it would require inventing a nonzero error source for Option A that does not exist). Instead this is the QA report's SECOND suggested repair: primary_metric reframed from raw accuracy to total shop time (Appendix F), so the dilemma's real tension -- cost/deadline/historical-precedent (Option B) vs. a known, named accuracy cost (Option B's ~12.5 cents / 150% tolerance overshoot, still fully disclosed in Appendix D and graded in Challenge D5) -- is what SPEC §2's balance test now measures. margin_pct = 100 x (total_A - total_B) / total_A = 100 x (52.33 - 50.13) / 52.33 = 4.2%. CORRECTED 2026-08-27 (Tier 2 P5 finding, see QA_REPORT.md and case.json.sensitivity_disclosure[]): the earlier note here claimed this margin was 'deliberately robust, not fragile' because doubling MA4 alone (a +100% widening move) only pushed the margin to ~16%. That check was real but one-directional -- it only tested MA4 getting SLOWER (which makes Option A slower and widens B's win). It did not test the narrowing direction SPEC §2/MCS-26's ±50% protocol actually requires: MA4 getting FASTER, or MA5 getting SLOWER. Because the per-fret gap (22 frets x 6s/fret ~= 2.2 min) is nearly as large as the entire 2.2-minute raw margin between the options, a ±50% flex in that narrowing direction DOES flip the winner to Option A: MA4 at -50% (10s) or MA5 at +50% (21s) each flip it (see sensitivity_model.py, verified via tier2_probes.py --probe 5 --flex 0.5). MA6 does not flip the verdict at either +/-50% bound. This instability is now disclosed, not eliminated, per case.json.sensitivity_disclosure[] (Category X on both MA4 and MA5) and in FACILITATOR.md's sensitivity note and Twist/discussion material -- the case no longer defends a 4.2% margin as more solid than it is. The accuracy figures (rule_of_18_cents_deviation_fret12, overshoot ratio/pct below) remain real, sourced-derived, and fully disclosed -- they are simply no longer what margin_pct is computed from.

accuracy_cost_context.note: Option B's disclosed, known, named accuracy cost (Appendix D) -- real and material to Challenge D5's recommendation, but as of the 2026-08-27 retune no longer the SPEC §2 balance-test primary metric, since Option A is exact by construction on this axis at every fret and no honest reframing within pure accuracy could ever produce a close margin. See balance.margin_note.

modeling_assumptions.text: Acceptable intonation tolerance a professional luthier targets, at the 12th fret
modeling_assumptions.basis: No single published professional trade standard states one hard number. Guitar-technician/luthier discussion threads converge on a working range of roughly 2-6 cents, and published psychoacoustic pitch-discrimination research places the just-noticeable difference for most listeners in a similar few-cents range. 5 cents sits inside that commonly cited range.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The case's answer is sensitive to this value (Rule of Eighteen's derived ~12.5-cent deviation at fret 12 sits outside this stated tolerance); the case does not print the resulting verdict here, per case-write SKILL.md's rule against stating the answer key in a Sensitivity/Why column.

modeling_assumptions.text: Number of frets on this neck
modeling_assumptions.basis: Falls inside the 21-24 fret range StewMac (S4) states is typical for a modern electric guitar; the exact count for this build is a shop/client choice, not itself a published standard.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Low -- does not change the per-fret math in D1-D4.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Consistent with the Overview's 'before the week is out' and a realistic fast custom-shop turnaround for a fretting job on an otherwise-finished neck.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Low for D1-D4; relevant context for D5's discussion of whether a re-fret is survivable within the deadline.

modeling_assumptions.text: Estimated hand/calculator time to compute one fret's position, Precision Method
modeling_assumptions.basis: Requires evaluating a fractional exponent (n/12) on a scientific calculator, then subtracting from 1 and multiplying by the scale length -- more keystrokes than a simple division, and an easy step to mis-key. No published source times this specific task; reasoned scenario estimate, added 2026-08-27 as part of the primary-metric retune (see case.json.balance.margin_note).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Dilemma-sensitive, corrected 2026-08-27 (see sensitivity_disclosure[] and QA_REPORT.md P5). The margin is robust to this value getting LARGER (widening, e.g. +100% keeps B winning by a wide margin), but the recommendation flips to Option A if this value gets roughly 50% SMALLER (10 seconds instead of 20) -- an apprentice who keys the exponent calculation faster than estimated closes the whole 2.2-minute gap. This is disclosed, not eliminated.

modeling_assumptions.text: Estimated hand/calculator time to compute one fret's position, Rule of Eighteen
modeling_assumptions.basis: Requires only a division of the remaining length by 18 followed by a running subtraction -- the same two-step shortcut proportional dividers were originally built to avoid doing by hand [S3: 'Use of the divider obviates the need to do a lot of mathematical division ... by hand in the days before calculators and computers']. No published source times this specific task; reasoned scenario estimate, added 2026-08-27 as part of the primary-metric retune.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Dilemma-sensitive, corrected 2026-08-27 (see sensitivity_disclosure[] and QA_REPORT.md P5). The margin is robust to this value getting SMALLER (widening B's advantage), but the recommendation flips to Option A if this value gets roughly 50% LARGER (21 seconds instead of 14) -- an apprentice who is slower at the running-subtraction shortcut than estimated erases the whole 2.2-minute gap. This is disclosed, not eliminated.

modeling_assumptions.text: Shared shop time to cut, install, and dress all 22 frets once marked (identical regardless of which method produced the marks)
modeling_assumptions.basis: Consistent with published professional repair-shop time-costing practice -- StewMac's own job-estimate example ('Guitar repair money talk: estimate hours, not dollars') lists roughly 0.6 hours for the fret-installation portion of a comparable repair job; this build additionally requires cutting fresh slots and dressing/leveling the frets, so 45 minutes is used as a round, order-of-magnitude estimate for the full sequence on this build's 22 frets. Added 2026-08-27 as part of the primary-metric retune.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This is the value that dominates total shop time for both options and is what keeps the total-shop-time margin close (see balance.margin_note) -- not printed with that framing in case.md's Modeling Assumptions block, per case-write SKILL.md's rule against stating a margin's result there.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: No published source times how long it takes a specific apprentice to key a fractional-exponent calculation on a scientific calculator for one fret; the true value exists in principle (it is directly measurable on a real apprentice, at a real bench) but is not publicly documented, so 20 seconds is a good-faith estimate from the closest public analogue -- the extra keystrokes a fractional exponent requires versus a simple division. This is the single dial whose -50% flex (10 seconds) flips the recommended winner from Option B to Option A; verified in cases/fret-board/sensitivity_model.py, tier2_probes.py --probe 5 --flex 0.5.

No published source times how long it takes a specific apprentice to run the Rule of Eighteen's division-and-running-subtraction by hand for one fret; the true value exists in principle but is not publicly documented, so 14 seconds is a good-faith estimate from the closest public analogue -- the two-step shortcut proportional dividers were built to replace [S3]. This is the second dial whose +50% flex (21 seconds) flips the recommended winner from Option B to Option A; verified in cases/fret-board/sensitivity_model.py, tier2_probes.py --probe 5 --flex 0.5.

P1 (blind cold-solve, fresh subagent, chose A with correct arithmetic and independently named MA1 as most sensitive), P2 (both-sides, neither collapses), P3 (trap-check, guide names the same trap), P4 (twist-integrity, twist genuinely unsettles a position and survives every stated assumption), and P6 (all 5 sources live-reachable, figures confirmed, S4 minor characterization looseness only) were all re-adjudicated fresh this pass and PASS.
